english.html: (a thing which the pure philosophers have esteemed above all others horrible and frightful <sup class="mk" data-key="l">l</sup>, even to the wicked <sup class="mk" data-key="m">m</sup>), being infinitely travailed and afflicted, would be so still more if he found himself pressed to remember so many and so many things, about which he might be too curiously and prolixly searched <sup class="mk" data-key="n">n</sup>. For who is there (said Cicero) from whom, when death approaches, the blood does not withdraw, and who does not turn white with fright and fear?

notes.original: Ariſtote au iij. liure des Ethiques.
notes.gloss: Death is the most terrible of all things, for it is the end.
The paradoxes on the wise man's indifference to death and the wicked man's fears; the passage not located.

english.html: Who is there, or how few are there, from whom, when death draws near, the timid blood does not flee back, and who does not grow pale with fear <sup class="mk" data-key="o">o</sup>?

notes.citation: Cicero, De finibus, book 5 (5.31), quoting an old tragic poet
notes.gloss: Quis est, aut quotusquisque, cui mors cum adpropinquet, / non refugiat timido sanguen atque exalbescat metu? The print has cùm non appropinquet, Non refugiat, a non displaced into the first line; translated from Cicero's text.

english.html: And in some other place: Who is there (he says) who, being on the point of dying, has his Spirit tranquil and at rest <sup class="mk" data-key="p">p</sup>?

notes.gloss: Cato on the fear of death in the old and the young; the sentence as Coras gives it is a paraphrase, the passage not located.

english.html: Before whom, on the sixteenth of September in the said year 1560, he confessed at full length his impudent and rash crime; nevertheless he declared that what had given him the first occasion to project his brazen and monstrous enterprise had been that, seven or eight years before, he being on his return from the camp of Picardy,

Picardy is a part of Belgic Gaul. Whereupon it must be understood that Gaul was formerly divided principally in two: namely into the Transalpine and the Cisalpine. The Cisalpine was called by the Romans that which took its beginning at the foot of the Alps and extended as far as the river Rubicon, the ancient boundary of Italy, which comes down from the Apennines and, passing by Rimini and Ravenna, enters the Adriatic sea.
